items.text: Do pretrained seismic models hold lab fault stress, friction and time to failure beyond what raw signal power gives, and does this grow with model size?
Pretrained seismic models will hold fault-state information beyond signal power that grows with model size, though signal power alone already gives lab stress R² 0.82 [rouet2018].
R² left after removing signal power rises steadily from smallest to largest model in both seeds, with smallest and largest confidence intervals not overlapping.
The size curve is flat, or pretrained probes sit within the confidence interval of random-init copies or the power baseline [rouet2018].

Probe frozen SeisLM models and random-init copies on Penn State lab stick-slip data for stress, friction and time to failure, beyond a power baseline. Check Norcia field data, and pretrain four model sizes in-domain to see if the signal grows.

Rouet-Leduc et al. read lab fault state from window statistics with a random forest (time-to-failure R² 0.89, stress >0.9) [rouet2017]; Li et al. probed Othello networks against randomised ones [li2022]. No probing of seismic foundation models found.

items.text: Can sparse autoencoders on a pretrained seismic waveform model recover known signal classes and hidden events better than spectrogram clustering or single neurons?
Sparse autoencoder features on SeisLM-large will find known signal classes and missed examples of them, beating spectrogram clustering and random-start autoencoders; a truly new class is unlikely.
Autoencoder features cost less to inspect than spectrogram clustering and single neurons, and beat the random-start autoencoder; rare classes get their own feature at 1% prevalence or below.
The pretrained autoencoder is about equal to the random-start one, or spectrogram clustering and single neurons match it; no class gets its own feature at 1% prevalence or below.

Train sparse autoencoders on three layers of SeisLM-large, score features against known labels, measure how rare a class can be and still get a feature, then scan Cascadia and Parkfield data, all on one H100 for about $700.
Goodfire's Evo 2 SAE work and InterPLM on protein models; no seismic SAE result was found, but no web search was run, so one may exist.
